newsitem.title: USA: Stock plans give employees a slice of the pie.
newsitem.headline: Stock plans give employees a slice of the pie.

text.p: Ann Keeling's employee stock ownership plan is making her rich -- not like at her last job where she received just a salary.

Employed as a $50,000-a-year account executive with the design firm of Libby Perszyk Kathman in Cincinnati, Keeling has earned an extra $22,500 in company stock in the two years since LPK adopted the plan.
LPK employs 100 workers who help to develop the brand identities of businesses like Microsoft, Heinz, Proctor & Gamble and Kroger.

"Her wage is not different from other companies in the field but the employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) makes the difference, and it's fully vested after three years," said LPK President Jerry Kathman.

"I've worked at several firms in our industry that were not ESOP companies," Keeling said, "and they were very tight-lipped regarding the financial status of the company. This created a great deal of underlying tension for me."

By contrast, she said, "owning 'a piece of the pie,' at LPK creates a sense of pride and motivation that impacts on my overall job satisfaction." Now she proudly wears a T-shirt displaying the LPK logo: a piece of pie.
Advocates of ESOPs say they turn employees into the home owners of the business world compared with peers who, as salaried hands, who may be thought of as renters.
A year before founder Mort Libby stepped aside, he decided that instead of selling LPK to a competitor, he'd sell it to his employees.
"We're not simply a bunch of nice people," said Kathman, who succeeded Libby, explaining the founder's rationale for the ESOP.

"We're in an industry of knowledge workers and in order to create a strong company -- where the pushing down of responsibility and empowerment is essential -- nothing would be more motivating than ownership across the board," Kathman said.

"The case of a retiring owner selling to employees has accounted for a good number of these (ESOP) plans over recent years," said Joseph Blasi, a professor in the school of management and labour relations at Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, NJ. He noted that more than 10,000 companies have ESOPs.

"Small business owners are very enthusiastic about preserving the identity of their business and selling it to the people who helped build it as well as having an opportunity to get a fair price for all their hard work and entrepreneurship," Blasi added.
The fair market value of LPK's internal stock was $39.50 when the ESOP was adopted. Boosted by strong sales, a year later it rose to $47 and at the end of 1996 it hit $54.
Prior to adopting the ESOP, LPK sales grew about 16 percent a year; in the two years since the plan was launched, they've risen 21 percent annually.

Keeling's stock, valued at $3,952 for 100 shares in 1994, was augmented with 164 new shares worth $7,725 which gave her $11,677 by the end of 1995. Then she got another 140 shares in 1996, raising her total ESOP nest egg to $22,500.
Prior to its adoption, LPK held numerous meetings to explain the ESOP concept to employees. "We published quarterly numbers, trying to empower people to understand all the issues," Kathman said.
Since LPK established its ESOP, Kathman said, turnover has virtually stopped. "One employee left us a year ago to move to the West Coast but we haven't lost anybody (else)," he said.
"We think this is a pillar of our success. Rather than working for some guy in the corner office, we all work together and the marketplace is rewarding us for that work."
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
